title: Asking the Archive

post.author: u/seance_lamp_imogen
post.title: Our house museum's séance answers from the family's letters. On Friday a visitor asked about Winifred, and the spirit remembered a goodbye she never had.

blocks.text: I'm a junior developer, and on Friday evenings I volunteer at Mallender House, a Victorian house museum on the edge of town. Twice a night we hold a séance in the back parlour. Mrs Dauntsey, our medium, a retired actor, turns the lamps down, and visitors ask the spirit of the house a question. The answer appears on a small screen hidden in the table lamp, and she reads it aloud.

The answers come from the family's archive: 2,300 letters, diaries and household accounts, 1858 to 1938, scanned and typed up by volunteers. In the summer I built the pipeline. My script split the archive into 2,760 passages of about 250 tokens and embedded each one. When a visitor asks something, the app embeds the question, takes the five passages closest to it by cosine similarity, and sends them to a model with the question and a short system prompt: answer as the house, and only from these passages. About 60 questions a night.

21:40  visitor  What did Winifred say about the night her brother left?
21:40  spirit   I walked him to the gate that night. He pressed my hand
                 and said he would write from the ship.

The visitor had read the plaque in the hall: Winifred Mallender, 1852 to 1919, whose brother Laurence left this house one night in March 1873 and never wrote home. Her portrait hangs on the landing, beside the window.
The visitor said: she never got a goodbye. That's the whole story of this house.

There were two Winifreds. The second, also Winifred Mallender, 1911 to 1990, was the first one's great-niece, named for her. In September 1933 her brother Osgood sailed for work abroad, and she wrote about the night he went. Sixty years apart, under the same name. On Saturday morning I ran Friday's question again and drew what came back.

blocks.caption: Drawn on Saturday morning from Friday's rerun. The five passages sent, by cosine similarity: the younger Winifred's letter of 9 September 1933 about the gate, 0.98, and about his trunk, 0.94; her diary of 9 September 1934, 0.90; Edmund Mallender's letter of 21 March 1873, 0.86; Harriet Mallender's household accounts for March 1873, a cab, 0.84. The elder Winifred's diary of 14 March 1873 came sixth, at 0.82, and was not sent. I looked up who wrote each one in the scan file names.

blocks.text: Nothing in the answer said which Winifred it was speaking for. The house wants the séance back next Friday. What do I change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in that parlour is haunted, though the lamp sounds lovely. What you built has a name: retrieval-augmented generation, RAG for short. The model has never read a Mallender letter; your app looks up passages and hands them over with the question, and the model writes from them. The number of passages it hands over is called k, and those passages are the top-k: yours is 5. Two questions. Which five went to the model on Friday, with their scores, and who wrote each one? And where did the elder Winifred's diary for March 1873 come, and how did you find out who wrote it?

replies.author: u/seance_lamp_imogen
replies.text: Top five: the younger Winifred's letter of 9 September 1933 about the gate, 0.98; the same letter about his trunk, 0.94; her diary a year later, 0.90; Edmund's letter of 21 March 1873, 0.86; Harriet's accounts for March 1873, a cab from the side gate, 0.84. The elder Winifred's diary of 14 March 1873 was sixth, at 0.82. I only know who wrote them because the scan file names say so. My script kept the text of each passage and nothing else, so the app never knew there were two of her.

comments.author: u/just_fine_tune_it_fairlie
comments.text: Retrieval is a crutch. You're running a search engine and hoping the model reads the right page. If you want a model to know your data, you fine-tune it on your data: all 2,300 items, a few training passes, and it knows the family the way someone who read every letter would. Both Winifreds, both brothers, who's who. That's how you make a model know things, and there's no search step left to get wrong.

replies.author: u/seance_lamp_imogen
replies.text: The county record office says there are two more boxes of accounts coming in the spring. What happens then?

replies.author: u/just_fine_tune_it_fairlie
replies.text: Another training run. Worth it for a model that just knows.

comments.author: u/gate_lilac_harrowby
comments.text: I was the visitor on Friday. Laurence Mallender was my great-great-grandfather. He reached Canada in the spring of 1873, married there, and never wrote home. My grandmother said he once told his children he left without saying goodbye to anyone, because he knew his sister would stop him. I went to the séance because I wanted to know what she said about that night. It gave me somebody else's goodbye.

replies.author: u/seance_lamp_imogen
replies.text: Her diary for that night is three lines long. I'll post you a copy, and the house would like you to come back on Friday.

reply.prompt: The house wants the séance back next Friday. What should Imogen change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Fine-tune a model on all 2,300 letters, diaries and account books, so the spirit knows the whole family the way someone who read everything would, and drop the search that picked the wrong Winifred.
options.verdict: It learns the family, and loses the sources
options.part2: I set the sim to a model fine-tuned on the archive, no retrieval. Friday's question came back the same: I walked him to the gate that night. Under it, nothing at all, because a fine-tuned model has no passage to point to. The writer filter and asking did nothing: there were no passages to filter, only what training left in the weights. On the six test questions it answered 3 from the right passage, the same as Friday, and I could only tell which three by checking every answer against the archive by hand. It costs $0.05 a night in tokens, but each box the record office sends would mean another training run.
options.senior: Fine-tuning changes how a model writes, and it can pick up facts, but usually unreliably, with no citation and no way to fix one letter without training again. It doesn't settle which Winifred either: the two are blended in the weights, where no filter can reach. For facts that must be right and checkable, retrieval puts the actual passage in front of the model.

options.text: Store who wrote each passage and when, and use it: ask which Winifred when a name fits two writers, and show it under every answer. Then test retrieval on questions whose right passages you know.
options.part2: I gave every passage its writer and date from the scan file names, switched on the writer filter, asking and sources, and kept the top 5. Friday's question: the spirit asked, Which Winifred do you mean: Winifred Mallender who wrote from 1868 to 1919, or Winifred Mallender who wrote from 1925 to 1938? The visitor said the elder. Only her passages were searched: the diary of 14 March 1873 at 0.82, her letter of 2 April 1873 at 0.78, her diary of 1883 at 0.64. The answer: There was no goodbye. I watched from the landing window, and he did not look back. Under it: Winifred Mallender (1852 to 1919), diary, 14 March 1873. On the six test questions the right passage came back 6 of 6 and the answer used it 6 of 6, at 1,670 tokens a question and $0.20 a night, as before. On Friday Mrs Dauntsey read it aloud, and the visitor looked up at the landing window.
options.senior: The answer is only as good as what was retrieved, and retrieval is only as good as what each passage carries. Keep who and when with every passage, show it under the answer, filter by it, and ask when a name fits two people. Then test retrieval on its own: did the right passage come back, and was it the one used?

options.text: Send the top 50 passages instead of the top 5. The elder Winifred's diary came sixth, so with fifty the right passage is surely in what the spirit reads, and it can work out which Winifred was meant.
options.verdict: The right passage arrives, and loses
options.part2: I set top k to 50. The elder Winifred's diary went to the model this time, sixth of 50 at 0.82. The answer didn't change: I walked him to the gate that night, from the younger Winifred's letter at 0.98, because the stand-in still answers from the best match it is given, and nothing told it which Winifred the visitor meant. On the test set the right passage now came back 6 of 6, and the answers still used it only 3 of 6. Each question went from 1,670 tokens to 12,920, and a night from $0.20 to $1.55.
options.senior: More passages raise the chance the right one is in the context, not the chance it gets used. The wrong Winifred still scores higher, and 45 more passages are noise to read past (case 4 of Season 2). Fix what decides which passage wins: who wrote it, and who was meant.

options.text: Skip the search and send the whole archive with every question. At 690,000 tokens it fits the model's window, so no passage can be missed, though each question costs more and takes longer.
options.verdict: Trade-off: it fits, at a price
options.part2: I sent the whole archive with every question: 690,420 tokens with the system prompt and the question, inside a 1,000,000-token window. Friday's answer was still the farewell at the gate: both Winifreds were in the context, and nothing said which was meant. 3 of 6 test answers came from the right passage. With asking switched on it got all 6, but each question cost $1.38 and a night $82.85, against $0.20. And the diary that matters sat somewhere in the middle of 690,000 tokens, where case 9 of Season 1 found models tend to use what they read less well.
options.senior: Sending everything is a real option for a small knowledge base: Anthropic suggests it under about 200,000 tokens, with prompt caching to cut the cost. At 690,000 tokens it is expensive on every question, slower, and buries the passage that matters. It also removes the one stage you can test on its own.

sim.title: Run the séance pipeline yourself
sim.lede: You're Imogen at seven on Saturday morning, rerunning Friday's question. The sim holds a teaching sample of 10 of the archive's 2,760 passages, each with its writer and date: three of the elder Winifred's, four of the younger Winifred's, one of Edmund's letters and two of Harriet's household accounts. Each passage and each question has a small embedding vector of four made-up numbers, all of length 10, so the cosine similarity is the dot product divided by 100 and every score is exact. The rest of the archive scores lower for every question here, a teaching assumption. There is no real model: a stand-in answers from the highest-scoring passage it is given and records which one. Pick where the knowledge comes from: the top k passages; the whole archive in the context; or a model fine-tuned on the archive, which by the sim's teaching rule answers from what it absorbed most strongly and has no passages to show. Set k, filter by the writer a question names, let the stand-in ask when a name fits two writers, and show sources under the answer. The test set is six questions whose right passages are known: did the right passage come back in the top k, and did the answer come from it? Tokens are teaching values: a 400-token system prompt, a 20-token question and 250 tokens a passage, at the teaching price of $2 per million input tokens, 60 questions a night.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start on Friday: top 5, no filter. The five sent score 0.98, 0.94, 0.90, 0.86 and 0.84; the elder Winifred's diary is sixth at 0.82, and the answer is the younger Winifred's farewell at the gate. The test set: 5 of 6 retrieved, 3 of 6 answered from the right passage, $0.20 a night. Set k to 50: 6 of 6 retrieved, still 3 of 6, $1.55. Back to 5, switch on the writer filter: the diary moves up to fourth and is sent, and the answer still comes from the gate. Switch on asking and sources: the stand-in asks which Winifred, searches only the elder's passages, and answers from her diary at 0.82, shown under the answer: 6 of 6 and 6 of 6. Pick the whole archive: 690,420 tokens a question, $82.85 a night. Pick fine-tuned: 3 of 6, and no sources at all.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the parlour is haunted. The model knew only what the app retrieved, and the app kept each passage's words but not who wrote them: two women called Winifred Mallender, sixty years apart, looked the same to the search, the younger one's farewell scored 0.98, the elder one's diary 0.82, and the stand-in answered from the best match it was given.

steps.title: A model knows its training data, up to a cutoff, and nothing private.
steps.text: A language model learns from a huge body of text and then stops learning: its weights are fixed. Anthropic's models overview lists two dates for each current model, a reliable knowledge cutoff, the date through which the model's knowledge is most extensive and reliable, and a training data cutoff, the broader range of data used. Nothing after that date is in the weights, and nothing that was never public: no model has read the Mallenders' letters. There are two ways to give a model knowledge. Change its weights by training it further, fine-tuning (case 2 of Season 1), or hand it the right documents with each question. Lewis and colleagues' 2020 paper, which named retrieval-augmented generation, put the problem plainly: large pre-trained language models have been shown to store factual knowledge in their parameters, but their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is still limited, and providing provenance for their decisions and updating their world knowledge remain open research problems. Fine-tuning is usually costly, slow to redo whenever the documents change, and can't say where an answer came from. Their answer: models which combine pre-trained parametric and non-parametric memory for language generation, where the non-parametric memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia, accessed with a pre-trained neural retriever. In plain words: keep the knowledge outside the model, look it up at question time, and put what you find in the context.

steps.title: The pipeline, end to end.
steps.text: RAG runs in two parts. Once, and again whenever the archive changes: ingest the documents, recording what each one is; chunk them into passages small enough to search and send; embed each passage (case 4 of Season 1); store the vectors with their text; and index them so the closest can be found quickly. Then on every question: embed the question the same way; retrieve the top-k passages by similarity; build the prompt, system prompt, passages and question, which is context engineering (case 4 of Season 2); generate the answer; and cite the passages it came from. Anthropic's 2024 contextual retrieval post describes the same steps: break down the knowledge base (the corpus of documents) into smaller chunks of text, use an embedding model to convert these chunks into vector embeddings that encode meaning, and store these embeddings in a vector database that allows for searching by semantic similarity. At runtime, the vector database is used to find the most relevant chunks, and the most relevant chunks are added to the prompt sent to the generative model. OpenAI's file search tool packages the same idea: it enables models to retrieve information in a knowledge base of previously uploaded files through semantic and keyword search. Imogen built every stage but one: her script threw away who wrote each passage.

steps.title: Every stage can go wrong, and this season takes them one at a time.
steps.text: Where a passage starts and ends decides what it can answer: a diary entry cut in two may match nowhere (case 2, chunking). Searching 2,760 vectors one by one is fine; searching millions needs an index that trades a little accuracy for speed (case 3). Meaning-based search can miss an exact word, a name or a code, that keyword search would catch (case 4). The order the passages come back in decides which one the model leans on, and a second, slower look can fix it (case 5). And the model may answer past its passages, or fail to say not found when nothing fits (case 6). This case is about the one thing under all of them: what goes in is what comes out.

steps.title: The answer is only as good as what was retrieved: keep who and when.
steps.text: Friday's question was embedded and compared with every passage. In the sim's teaching sample the five closest were the younger Winifred's letter of 9 September 1933 about the gate at 0.98, the same letter about his trunk at 0.94, her diary a year later at 0.90, Edmund's letter of 21 March 1873 at 0.86 and Harriet's accounts for March 1873 at 0.84. The elder Winifred's diary of 14 March 1873 came sixth at 0.82, so it never reached the model. Nothing was broken: both women wrote about a brother leaving at night, and an embedding captures what a passage is about, not who wrote it. The model, or the sim's stand-in, wrote from the best passage it was given, and with no writer or date attached, the answer couldn't say whose words they were. The fix is metadata: keep each passage's writer and date with it, from ingest on. Then use it three ways. Filter by it, a metadata filter: search only the writer the question names. Ask when it's ambiguous: Winifred fits two writers here, so the stand-in asks which, and searches only her passages, where the 1873 diary comes first. Show it: put the writer and date under every answer, so a reader can check. OpenAI's file search supports the same thing: you can filter the search results based on the metadata of the files. Raising k doesn't help: at 50 the diary is sent, sixth, and the answer still comes from the 0.98 letter.

steps.title: Test retrieval on its own, before the answer.
steps.text: An answer can go wrong in retrieval or in generation, and you can't fix what you can't tell apart. So test retrieval separately, with a set of questions whose right passages you know, written by someone who knows the archive. For each question, check two things: did the right passage come back in the top k, and was it the one the answer used? That first number is the retrieval hit rate. On Friday's settings, the sim's six test questions found the right passage in the top 5 for 5 of 6, and the answer used it for 3 of 6. Top 50 made the first number 6 of 6 and left the second at 3: a hit rate at k can look fine while the answers stay wrong. With the writer filter and asking, both were 6 of 6, at the same 1,670 tokens a question. Run the set before any change to the pipeline, and grow it whenever a visitor finds a new way to be misunderstood. Season 5 builds evals properly.

diagram.aria: The RAG pipeline. Top row, once and whenever the archive changes: ingest, documents with writer and date; chunk, into passages that keep their metadata; embed, each passage to a vector; store and index, vectors, text and metadata. Bottom row, on every question: the question, embedded the same way; retrieve, the top k, filtered by metadata; build the prompt, passages then the question; generate and cite, the answer with its sources. Store and index feeds retrieve.

notes.text: once, and whenever the archive changes

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right, then the bottom row. The top row runs once and again whenever the archive changes: take the documents in with their writer and date, split them into passages that keep that metadata, embed each one, and store the vectors, text and metadata in a searchable index. The bottom row runs on every question: embed it the same way, retrieve the top k passages, filtered by metadata where the question names someone, build the prompt with the passages before the question, and generate an answer with its sources shown.

fix.title: The fix: keep who and when, use it, and test retrieval
fix.text: Re-ingest the archive with each item's writer and date, from the scan file names, and keep them with every passage it is split into. At question time, filter by the writer a question names. When a name fits more than one writer, as Winifred does here, ask which one before searching, and search only her passages. Show the writer and date of each passage used under every answer, so Mrs Dauntsey, or anyone, can check it. Keep k small. Then write a test set: questions whose right passages someone who knows the archive has marked, including every name that fits two people. For each, check that the right passage comes back in the top k and that the answer uses it, and run the set before any change to the pipeline. In the sim that is the elder Winifred's diary at 0.82 and the answer There was no goodbye, 6 of 6 retrieved and 6 of 6 answered from the right passage, at the same 1,670 tokens a question and $0.20 a night, against Friday's 5 of 6 and 3 of 6.

limits: Metadata is only as good as whoever records it. If a scan's file name had the wrong year, or a letter signed only A. was guessed wrong, the filter would hide the right passage with full confidence. Check the metadata, keep where each value came from, and let the test set catch the guesses.

Asking costs a turn, and not every ambiguity is a name: the night her brother left could mean two nights even for one Winifred. Ask only when the metadata shows a real split, and fall back to showing both with their dates. Filtering also can't help a passage that never matched at all; that is chunking and search, the next four cases.

The sim is a teaching simplification: four-number vectors, a sample of 10 passages, and a stand-in that answers from the top passage. Real models read every passage they are sent and may blend them, which is how a wrong Winifred's details can turn up in a right Winifred's answer; case 6 covers grounding. Standards readiness: the archive includes living descendants' family details, so wherever the GDPR applies to such data, sending a provider only the passages a question needs is data minimisation (case 9 of Season 1). Build it in now, not at audit time.

explain.seniorTake: A model knows only its training, so to answer from your documents you either retrain it or hand it the right passages at question time. Retrieval wins when the facts change, must be cited, or are private. But the answer can only be as good as what comes back, so keep who and when with every passage, use it to filter and to show sources, and test retrieval on its own with questions whose right passages you know.

realWorld.title: Lewis et al.: retrieval-augmented generation, 2020
realWorld.text: Patrick Lewis and eleven colleagues introduced the name in Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (arXiv 2005.11401, first posted May 2020). The abstract says large pre-trained language models have been shown to store factual knowledge in their parameters, but their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is still limited, and providing provenance for their decisions and updating their world knowledge remain open research problems. RAG models, it says, are models which combine pre-trained parametric and non-parametric memory for language generation, where the non-parametric memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia, accessed with a pre-trained neural retriever.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: the pipeline, in their words
realWorld.text: Anthropic's Introducing Contextual Retrieval post (September 2024) says that for an AI model to be useful in specific contexts, it often needs access to background knowledge, and that RAG is a method that retrieves relevant information from a knowledge base and appends it to the user's prompt. Its steps: break down the knowledge base into smaller chunks of text, use an embedding model to convert these chunks into vector embeddings that encode meaning, and store these embeddings in a vector database that allows for searching by semantic similarity; at runtime, the vector database is used to find the most relevant chunks, which are added to the prompt. It also notes that if your knowledge base is smaller than 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages of material), you can just include the entire knowledge base in the prompt. The post's own technique is case 7 of this season.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: file search
realWorld.text: OpenAI's file search guide describes a tool in the Responses API that enables models to retrieve information in a knowledge base of previously uploaded files through semantic and keyword search, using vector stores. It says you can filter the search results based on the metadata of the files, and that you can customize the number of results you want to retrieve, which can help reduce both token usage and latency, but may come at the cost of reduced answer quality. Search results are not returned by default, and the output contains the response along with the file citations.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: knowledge cutoffs
realWorld.text: Anthropic's models overview lists, for every current model, a reliable knowledge cutoff, the date through which the model's knowledge is most extensive and reliable, and a training data cutoff, the broader range of data used. Anything after those dates, and anything private, has to reach the model through its context.

realWorld.title: Lost in the middle, once more
realWorld.text: Case 9 of Season 1 met Liu and colleagues' 2023 finding: in long inputs, models tended to use relevant information at the start or end better than information in the middle. Sending the whole archive puts the elder Winifred's diary somewhere inside 690,000 tokens.

asked: What is RAG, and when would you use it instead of fine-tuning?
Walk me through a RAG pipeline.
How do you know retrieval is working?
interview.answer: A model knows only its training data, up to a cutoff, and nothing private. RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, gives it knowledge at question time instead: look up the passages relevant to the question and put them in the context with it, so the model answers from them and can cite them. I'd use RAG when the facts are private, change often, or have to be checked, because updating means ingesting new documents, not training again, and every answer can show its sources. I'd use fine-tuning for how a model behaves, its style, format or a narrow task, not for facts that must be right and citable; often the two go together. If the whole knowledge base is small, a couple of hundred thousand tokens, sending all of it with prompt caching can be simpler. The pipeline has two halves. Offline: ingest the documents with their metadata, who, when, what kind; chunk them into passages; embed each one; store the vectors, text and metadata; and index them. Per question: embed the question with the same model, retrieve the top k by similarity, filtered by metadata where the question allows, build the prompt with the passages before the question, generate, and cite. Each stage can fail on its own: chunk boundaries, the index, meaning versus exact keywords, ranking, and grounding. To know retrieval works, I test it apart from generation: a set of questions whose right passages are known, including ambiguous names and dates. For each I check whether the right passage comes back in the top k, the hit rate, and whether it ranks first or is the one the answer used. Then I run that set before every change, and add every real failure to it.

terms.def: A historic house kept much as it was and opened to visitors, often with the family's own papers and furniture.
A person who claims to pass messages between the living and the dead, usually at a séance. Mrs Dauntsey plays one.
A family's written record of what it spent, day by day: coal, candles, wages, a cab.
A digital image of a paper page, made so it can be stored, typed up and searched.
A small sign fixed to a wall that tells visitors about a person or event.
The flat floor at the top of a flight of stairs, or between two flights.
Here, someone paid to carry goods and luggage by cart from one place to another.
Old British money: s is shillings and d is pence. 4s is four shillings; 2s 6d is two shillings and sixpence.
A public archive, often run by a county, that keeps old documents and accepts donations of family papers.
A short piece of a longer document, stored, embedded and searched on its own. Imogen's are about 250 tokens.
One piece made by splitting a document for retrieval. This case calls them passages. How to split well is case 2 of this season.
To take documents into a system: read them, record what each one is, and get them ready to split and store.
The k highest-scoring results of a search. Imogen's app sends the top 5 passages, so k is 5.
The documents a RAG system answers from. Anthropic's post also calls it the corpus.
The text a model learned from before it was released. Its weights hold what it picked up, and nothing later.
The date a model's training data stops, so it knows little or nothing newer. Anthropic lists a reliable knowledge cutoff and a training data cutoff.
The part of a RAG system that searches the stored passages and returns the closest ones for a question.
Here, the model writing its answer from the question and the passages it was given.
What a model knows from its parameters, its weights, learned in training. Lewis et al.'s term.
Knowledge kept outside the model, such as passages in an index, looked up and handed to it at question time. Lewis et al.'s term.
Where a piece of information came from. For an answer, the passages and documents it was based on.
An index of embedding vectors that can be searched for the vectors closest to a query. Lewis et al. built one of Wikipedia.
A task that needs facts a person would have to look up, such as answering questions about one family's archive.
A search rule that keeps only results whose metadata matches, such as passages by one writer or from one decade.
Fitting more than one meaning. Winifred is ambiguous in this archive: two writers have that name.
Here, the writer, date and document of each passage an answer used, shown under the answer so a reader can check it.
Questions whose right passages someone has marked in advance, run to check that the search brings those passages back.
The share of test questions whose right passage comes back in the top k. Friday's settings: 5 of 6.
The retrieval hit rate for a given k. It says the right passage arrived, not that the answer used it.
OpenAI's name for a store of uploaded files, split into chunks and embedded, that its file search tool searches.
OpenAI's tool in the Responses API that searches uploaded files by meaning and by keywords and returns the passages with citations.
A company's document of its rules and policies for staff, such as leave, expenses and travel.
An international standard for quality management systems. A company can be audited and certified against it.
ISO 9001's term for the documents and records an organisation must keep and control, such as its policies.
An evening project in this course where you build part of a real system yourself, step by step.
The website monitoring service you build across Build Nights, with an AI incident copilot added in the crossover season.
Natural language processing: getting computers to work with human language, such as answering questions or translating.
The free online encyclopedia written by volunteers. Lewis et al. used its articles as the documents to retrieve from.
A sitting room for receiving guests in an old house.
Here, the charity that owns and runs the house museum, and the members of its board.
The house of a parish's vicar, a Church of England priest. Its papers often record the parish's births, marriages and deaths.
An assistant that helps an on-call engineer find the likely cause of an incident from logs, deploy events and runbooks.

atWork: Find an assistant at work that answers from your documents: a handbook bot, an internal search, a support helper. A common incident: a handbook bot tells staff the old travel policy, because last year's version and this year's sit side by side in its store, word for word alike except the numbers, and nothing under the answer says which version it came from. Look at what each stored passage carries besides its text. Does it know which document it came from, which version, when it took effect, who owns it, and whether it was replaced? Keep those as metadata, filter out replaced versions, and show the document, version and date under every answer. Then write a retrieval test set: twenty questions whose right passages the policy owners mark, including every policy that changed this year, and check that the right passage comes back and is the one used before any change goes live. Standards-readiness note: if your company holds or is pursuing ISO 9001:2015 certification, clause 7.5.3 (control of documented information) asks that documented information be available and suitable for use where and when it is needed and that changes to it be controlled; a bot answering from a superseded policy is the kind of gap an auditor raises, so build version metadata in now rather than at audit time. In the crossover season, Nightwatch's Build Night X1 builds exactly this: an incident copilot with RAG over runbooks, whose answers cite the log lines and runbook sections they used.

recall.prompt: Your company's support assistant answers customers from 4,000 help articles: the top 5 passages go to a model with the question. Two of your apps each have a feature called Sync, and one of them was retired in 2023. Customers asking about Sync often get instructions for the retired one, and nothing in the answer says which app it is about. A teammate wants to fine-tune a model on all the articles instead. What do you tell them, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Fine-tuning won't fix it: it is costly to redo on every change, gives no sources, and blends the two features in the weights
Keep metadata with every passage (which app, version, retired or not) and filter by it, or ask when the name fits two apps
Show the sources under each answer, so readers and staff can see which article it came from
Test retrieval separately: questions with known right passages, checking they come back and are used

recall.model: I'd tell them fine-tuning won't fix it. It's costly to redo every time an article changes, it can't cite which article an answer came from, and the two Syncs would just be blended in the weights, where nothing can separate them. The problem is retrieval: the passages carry their text but not which app they belong to or that one was retired. I'd re-ingest the articles with metadata on every passage: the app, the version, and whether it's retired. Then filter out retired articles, filter by app when the customer's app is known, and ask the customer which app when Sync fits two. I'd show sources under each answer, the article and its date, so customers and staff can see which article it came from. And I'd build a test set of questions with known right passages, including every name shared by two apps, and check the right passage comes back in the top k and is the one used, measuring that hit rate before and after any change.

recall.prompt: Why did the séance answer Friday's question with a farewell at the gate?
options: The model invented it, a hallucination from novels it was trained on
The five passages sent were the younger Winifred's and others; the elder's diary came sixth at 0.82
The script cut the elder Winifred's diary entry in half, so neither half matched
The vector index skipped the diary to save time, as fast indexes sometimes do
recall.why: Retrieval sent the younger Winifred's letter about the gate (0.98), the same letter about his trunk (0.94), her 1934 diary (0.90), Edmund's letter (0.86) and Harriet's accounts (0.84). The elder Winifred's diary was sixth at 0.82 and never reached the model, and with no writer or date kept, nothing said whose farewell it was. The words came from a real letter, not from training, and the diary was whole and found, just ranked sixth.

recall.prompt: A teammate asks: what is RAG, and when would you use it instead of fine-tuning? Answer in plain words.

keyIdeas.idea: A model knows only its training data, up to a cutoff, and nothing private
RAG looks up relevant passages at question time and puts them in the context with the question
Use RAG when facts change or must be cited: updating means adding documents, and answers can show sources
Fine-tuning suits behaviour, style or format, and is costly and slow to redo

recall.model: A model only knows its training data, up to a cutoff date, and nothing private, like our own documents. RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, looks up the passages relevant to a question at question time and puts them in the context with the question, so the model answers from them. I'd use it when the facts are private, change often, or must be cited: updating means adding new documents, not retraining, and every answer can show its sources. Fine-tuning is better for behaviour, a style, a format or a narrow task, and it's costly and slow to redo every time the facts change.

recall.prompt: In a RAG pipeline, what happens on every question, in order?
options: Chunk the documents, embed them, store them, then generate the answer
Generate an answer, then search the documents to find passages that support it
Embed the question, retrieve the top k passages, build the prompt, generate and cite
Fine-tune the model on the question's topic, then answer from what it learned
recall.why: Ingesting, chunking, embedding and storing happen once, and again when the documents change. On each question the app embeds it with the same embedding model, retrieves the top k passages by similarity, filtered by metadata where it can, builds the prompt with the passages before the question, generates the answer, and cites the passages used.

recall.prompt: How should Imogen check that retrieval itself is working, apart from the answers?
options: Run questions whose right passages are known, and check each comes back in the top k and is used
Read a week of the spirit's answers and count how many visitors seemed satisfied
Raise k until every right passage is somewhere in what gets sent to the model
Check that every passage in the store has an embedding of the right length
recall.why: A retrieval test set separates the two failures: did the right passage come back (the hit rate at k), and was it the one the answer used? Satisfied visitors don't know the archive, raising k made Friday's hit rate 6 of 6 while the answers stayed 3 of 6, and well-formed embeddings say nothing about which passage wins.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The séance still asks which Winifred, and our check questions have grown to 30; all 30 pass. Now the parish has lent us the old vicarage's papers, 9,000 more items, and the trust wants the spirit to answer from both archives. Mrs Dauntsey has asked for one change too: no sources on the screen in the lamp, because reading out a writer and date breaks the spell. And a trustee says that with the model's million-token window we could skip retrieval and send both archives every time.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What would you tell the trust, Mrs Dauntsey and the trustee, and what would you build?

keyIdeas.idea: Ingest the vicarage papers with the same metadata, plus which archive each passage came from, and filter or ask by it
Keep the sources recorded and visible somewhere, to staff or on request, even if the lamp doesn't read them out
Both archives won't fit or will cost too much every time: keep retrieval
Extend the test set with vicarage questions and new shared names, and run it before going live

coldCase.model: Ingest the vicarage papers the same way, with the writer and date on every passage, plus which archive it came from, and filter by it: a question about the Mallenders searches their papers, and a name that turns up in both, a vicar and a Mallender called Laurence, gets the same question back, which one? For Mrs Dauntsey, keep the sources out of the lamp if she likes, but keep them: record each answer's passages in a log, show them on a staff screen, and have a printed card for any visitor who asks afterwards. For the trustee: 9,000 more items on top of 690,000 tokens won't fit a million-token window, and even if it did, every question costs dollars and would bury the passage that matters in the middle. Keep retrieval. Then extend the test set with vicarage questions and every name the two archives share, and rerun it before going live.

sources.title: Lewis, Perez, Piktus, Petroni, Karpukhin, Goyal, Küttler, Lewis, Yih, Rocktäschel, Riedel and Kiela, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, arXiv 2005.11401, first submitted 22 May 2020 (v4, 12 April 2021): large pre-trained language models have been shown to store factual knowledge in their parameters; their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is still limited; providing provenance for their decisions and updating their world knowledge remain open research problems; models which combine pre-trained parametric and non-parametric memory for language generation; the non-parametric memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia, accessed with a pre-trained neural retriever

Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval, Anthropic Engineering, published 19 September 2024, read 11 October 2026: for an AI model to be useful in specific contexts, it often needs access to background knowledge; RAG retrieves relevant information from a knowledge base and appends it to the user's prompt; break down the knowledge base (the corpus of documents) into smaller chunks of text; use an embedding model to convert these chunks into vector embeddings that encode meaning; store these embeddings in a vector database that allows for searching by semantic similarity; at runtime the vector database is used to find the most relevant chunks, which are added to the prompt sent to the generative model; if your knowledge base is smaller than 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages of material), you can just include the entire knowledge base in the prompt

OpenAI, File search (developer docs), read 11 October 2026: file search is a tool available in the Responses API; it enables models to retrieve information in a knowledge base of previously uploaded files through semantic and keyword search; vector stores; you can filter the search results based on the metadata of the files; you can customize the number of results you want to retrieve, which can help reduce both token usage and latency, but may come at the cost of reduced answer quality; search results are not returned by default; the response comes with the file citations

Anthropic, Models overview (Claude Platform docs), read 11 October 2026: each current model lists a reliable knowledge cutoff, the date through which the model's knowledge is most extensive and reliable, and a training data cutoff, the broader range of data used; current models have a 1M-token context window

Liu, Lin, Hewitt, Paranjape, Bevilacqua, Petroni and Liang, Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts, arXiv 2307.03172, 2023: performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and degrades when it is in the middle (covered in case 9 of Season 1)
ISO 9001:2015, Quality management systems, Requirements: clause 7.5.3, control of documented information

Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation, Article 5(1)(c): personal data shall be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimisation)
